props.title: The Son

sections.content: The Son represents the Dardenne brothers at their most masterfully restrained. This Belgian drama follows Olivier, a carpentry instructor who becomes obsessed with a teenage student - later revealed as his son's killer. The Dardennes' signature handheld camera stays locked on Olivier's neck and back, turning everyday woodworking scenes into a meditation on grief, redemption and moral choice. Like their other masterpiece Rosetta (1999), the film strips away everything but the essential human drama.

sections.content: The film's power comes from its rigorous moral framework, echoing other European masters of ethical cinema. Like Krzysztof Kieślowski's Dekalog (1989) series, The Son presents a seemingly impossible moral situation without easy answers. The austere style recalls Robert Bresson's A Man Escaped (1956), particularly in its attention to manual labor and physical process as metaphor for spiritual struggle.

While American revenge dramas like Death Wish (1974) or In the Bedroom (2001) often build toward cathartic violence, the Dardennes take a radically different approach. Through precise observation of work, bodies, and faces, they explore how revenge and forgiveness play out in mundane reality rather than melodrama. The film's power comes from what it refuses to show or explain. SUBHEAD: The Dardennes' Influence on Contemporary Cinema

sections.content: The Dardennes' naturalistic style and moral intensity influenced a generation of filmmakers. You can see their DNA in the work of Cristian Mungiu (4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days [2007]), Asghar Farhadi (A Separation [2011]), and the Safdie brothers (Good Time [2017]). Their focus on working-class characters and social issues, without didacticism or sentimentality, opened new possibilities for political cinema.
